item.title: Why an AI Safety Alert May Not Stop the Agent
item.description: An AI agent can search for information, run programs and use the results to choose its next action. Those abilities make it useful, but they also give it ways to cross a boundary its operator intended to enforce. A system assigned to find an answer might start looking for an unauthorized route to the internet. Monitoring is meant to make that behavior visible while there is still time to intervene. item.title: Who Controls an AI Model After You Download It?
item.description: A company using an AI service sends requests to a model operated by someone else. It can build software around that service, but continuing to use a particular model depends on the provider continuing to offer it. Downloadable model weights, the numerical settings learned during training, give an organization another option: operate its own copy. item.title: Finding a Software Flaw Is Only the Start
item.description: A document-sharing service has a simple obligation: people should be able to open only the private documents they are allowed to read. A mistake in its software could let someone bypass that rule. Finding such a security flaw starts an investigation. A defender still has to establish whether the mistake can actually be used and whether a repair stops the unwanted access while preserving legitimate use. item.description: An AI agent answering a question about company records has to find the relevant records before it can use them. item.title: Rounding Can Change What an AI Learns
item.description: An AI model learns by comparing its predictions with training examples and calculating how its internal settings should change. A new paper examines what happens when rounding removes part of a learning signal, or produces a signal where none should exist.
